job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 — Loophole and Drafting Review (manager's amendment text, Oct. 6, 2026)

**Sec. 2(1)(A) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"**

1. **§ 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** The tonnage threshold attaches to each vessel, not to the operator, project, or license area. An operator can run three or four vessels each lifting just under 10,000 t/yr, or rotate vessels through a site, and never engage in "commercial deep seabed mining" at all.

2. **§ 2(1)(A), the 10,000-ton floor.** Even per vessel, 10,000 tons a year is substantial industrial activity (TMC's 2022 pilot trial lifted roughly 3,000 tons), so the bill exempts the entire pilot/pre-commercial phase outright. Seabed damage also tracks the area swept by collectors, not tons lifted, so a low-recovery, high-disturbance operation falls outside the definition.

3. **§ 2(1)(A), "per year."** Undefined — calendar year, license year, or rolling 12 months? On a calendar reading, 9,999 tons in December and 9,999 tons in January is nearly 20,000 tons in eight weeks with no violation; the text also doesn't say wet or dry weight, or nodules versus total material lifted.

4. **§ 2(1)(A), "recovery," "mineral resources," "from the seabed."** None is defined. In a riser system, the collector vehicle (not a vessel) picks up nodules, a production vessel lifts them, and a bulk carrier takes them away — it's unclear which "vessel" "recovers." "Mineral resources" could be read narrowly to exclude sulfides and crusts, or broadly to sweep in deepwater oil and gas (OCSLA treats hydrocarbons as minerals), inviting opposition and an overbreadth argument.

5. **§ 2(1)(A), threshold timing.** Because the prohibited act is defined by an annual total, no violation exists until the 10,001st ton — enforcement can begin only after the damage is done, and it is unclear how a per-day penalty (§ 5(a)) is computed against an annual quantity.

**Sec. 2(1)(B) — Catch-all**

6. **§ 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The term is never defined anywhere in the Act — Commerce (NOAA), State (§ 6), or Interior? Until fixed, the catch-all is inoperative and a court could not apply it.

7. **§ 2(1)(B), discretionary trigger.** The catch-all only works if the Secretary affirmatively makes a determination, with no mandate, deadline, petition process, or standard beyond "comparable." An unsympathetic administration can simply never act, collapsing the definition to subparagraph (A) and its loopholes.

8. **§ 2(1)(B) with § 5(b).** Tying 10-year felony liability to an unspecified official's "comparable risk" judgment, with no rulemaking, publication, or notice requirement, invites void-for-vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges, and every determination will draw an APA suit.

**Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person"**

9. **§ 2(2), "corporation."** LLCs, limited partnerships, trusts, joint ventures, and other non-corporate entities — the standard project vehicles — are not covered, nor are entities organized under federal law, D.C., or the territories ("a State" is undefined).

10. **§ 2(2), foreign subsidiaries and controlled entities.** A U.S. company can mine through a Bermuda or Marshall Islands subsidiary with no liability; the definition has no "owned or controlled by a U.S. person" language of the kind used in OFAC and export-control regimes. (The leading company in the sector is already Canadian-incorporated with U.S. subsidiaries.)

11. **§ 2(2), individuals.** Lawful permanent residents and U.S. nationals are omitted, as are foreign nationals who direct operations from U.S. offices (unless caught by "in the United States," see item 14).

12. **§ 2(2) and § 3(a), U.S.-flag vessels.** The bill never reaches vessels flagged in the United States or operating from U.S. ports — flag-state jurisdiction is the normal and strongest hook for high-seas enforcement, and it is missing entirely.

**Sec. 2(3) — "Covered vessel"**

13. **§ 2(3), 5,000 GT and "equipped for the recovery."** Vessels under 5,000 GT, support/transshipment/processing vessels, and vessels with modular equipment temporarily removed escape the registry, and "operator" is undefined. Because § 2(1)(A) has no tonnage element, a vessel can violate § 3 without ever having to register under § 4.

**Sec. 3(a) — Prohibition**

14. **§ 3(a), "in the United States."** "United States" is undefined and would ordinarily not include the EEZ or outer continental shelf, so a foreign company mining the U.S. EEZ (e.g., off American Samoa or the CNMI, where lease interest is active) is not covered unless it is a U.S. person.

15. **§ 3(a), "engage in."** Only the direct actor is reached: financing, insuring, chartering, contracting for, directing, transporting, processing, landing in U.S. ports, or purchasing the output are all untouched, and there is no aiding/abetting, conspiracy, or "cause to" language. There is also no import ban, no federal procurement bar, and no bar on EXIM/DFC financing, so U.S. markets and capital remain fully open to foreign mining.

16. **§ 3(a), "person."** Undefined, and the ordinary presumption excludes the sovereign, so federal agencies are not bound — NOAA could still issue DSHMRA permits and DoD could still contract for seabed minerals.

17. **§ 2(1)(A) with § 3(a), who is liable.** The definition is vessel-centric but the prohibition is person-centric, leaving it unclear whether the owner, operator, charterer, master, parent company, or individual crew bears liability; defendants will argue the parent is insulated by the corporate veil.

**Sec. 3(b) — Existing operations**

18. **§ 3(b), "mining conducted under an exploration license."** Exploration licenses (DSHMRA or ISA contracts) do not authorize commercial recovery, so this clause converts every existing exploration authorization into a permanent commercial-mining exemption. This is the single largest hole in the bill and effectively swallows § 3(a) for every incumbent.

19. **§ 3(b), no issuer specified.** Any license from any government or from the ISA (which has issued 30-plus exploration contracts) qualifies; a sponsoring state can grandfather its clients by issuing paper.

20. **§ 3(b), no time, scope, or transfer limits.** The exemption never expires and says nothing about renewals, extensions, area amendments, or assignments to new holders — a renewed or transferred license will be argued to have been "issued before" enactment.

21. **§ 3(b), pre-enactment rush.** Keying to the date of enactment creates an open window between now and signature to obtain licenses that will be grandfathered forever, at a time when NOAA has been directed (EO 14285) to expedite DSHMRA licensing; the cutoff should be the date of introduction or committee action.

**Sec. 3(c) — Environmental assessment**

22. **§ 3(c).** No tonnage cap, no approval, no definition, no reporting: industry pilot collector trials are routinely framed as environmental test mining, and "for the purpose of" doesn't say whether that must be the sole purpose or merely one purpose. An operator can lift unlimited quantities under an assessment label.

**Sec. 4 — Registry**

23. **§ 4(a)–(b), no penalty.** § 5 penalizes only violations of § 3, so failure to register, failure to report, and false certification carry no consequence under this Act; there is also no deadline for registration.

24. **§ 4(b), content of reports.** Reports need only "describe" activities — no requirement to report tonnage, location, depth, dates, flag, or beneficial ownership, i.e., exactly the data needed to enforce the 10,000-ton threshold. Reports are self-certified with no inspection, observer, vessel-tracking, or audit authority, and no public disclosure.

25. **§ 4(a), jurisdiction.** The registry has no jurisdictional limit, purporting to bind every covered vessel worldwide; that is unenforceable against foreign operators and hands challengers an extraterritoriality argument. NOAA is also given no rulemaking authority to implement it.

**Sec. 5 — Penalties**

26. **§ 5(a) with § 8.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. That is an internal contradiction and, read literally, punishes conduct before the prohibition was in force — an ex post facto/due process problem and an obvious litigation target.

27. **§ 5(a), penalty structure.** A per-day penalty keyed to an annual tonnage violation can be argued to attach to a single day (the day the threshold is crossed), i.e., one $1 million exposure. Even at $1 million per day, a full-scale operation projected to gross well over $1 billion a year could treat it as a cost of doing business; there is no minimum, no per-ton alternative, no disgorgement, and no forfeiture of vessels or minerals.

28. **§ 5, no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to investigate, board, assess, or sue; there is no injunctive-relief authority, no administrative procedure, no judicial-review provision, and no citizen suit.

29. **§ 5(b), "willfully."** Specific-intent liability is a high bar; corporate defendants cannot be imprisoned and face only title 18 fines (generally $500,000 per count or twice the gain), and there is no responsible-corporate-officer provision.

**Sec. 6 — International agreement**

30. **§ 6.** "Seek to negotiate" is hortatory with no report-back, and it is ambiguous whether 18 months is the deadline to begin or to conclude. "Equivalent to section 3" would also export the § 3(b) and § 3(c) loopholes into any treaty.

**Sec. 7 — Duration**

31. **§ 7(a) vs. § 7(b).** The two subsections conflict: (a) says the ban lasts until an affirmative science-based finding, while (b) terminates the whole Act in 10 years regardless. (b) controls, which makes the National Academies mechanism meaningless.

32. **§ 7(b), the sunset itself.** A "Prohibition Act" that expires automatically tells companies — whose exploration licenses already run 15 years — simply to wait, and gives investors a date certain. It should be struck or made contingent on the § 7(a) finding.

33. **§ 7(b), no savings clause.** "Cease to have effect" could be read to extinguish pending enforcement actions and liability for pre-sunset violations.

34. **§ 7(a), the finding mechanism.** A joint resolution is surplusage (Congress can always legislate), "serious harm" is undefined, nothing requires the Academies report to actually support the finding, and no study is commissioned or funded.

**Sec. 8 — Effective date**

35. **§ 8.** The 180-day delay creates a window for accelerated recovery and licensing before the ban bites, compounds items 21 and 26, and includes no interim freeze on new federal licenses, permits, or leases.

**Cross-cutting omissions**

36. **No conforming amendments to DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) or OCSLA.** NOAA keeps its statutory authority to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, and BOEM keeps leasing authority, so the bill creates dueling statutes; permittees will argue a later permit is an implied exception. The bill should expressly suspend that authority.

37. **No severability clause.** Given the vulnerable provisions (items 8, 25, 26), a successful challenge to one could take down the Act.

38. **No general definitions or implementation provisions.** "Person," "Secretary," "United States," "State," "operator," "recovery," "mineral resources," and "year" are all undefined, and there is no rulemaking authority, appropriation, or implementation deadline.

---

**If the committee will only take a handful of fixes at markup**, the ones that matter most are: strike or rewrite § 3(b) (item 18), move the tonnage threshold from per-vessel to per-operator/project or replace it with an activity-based definition (items 1–2), broaden "U.S. person" to owned-or-controlled entities and U.S.-flag vessels (items 10, 12), strike the § 7(b) sunset (item 32), and define "the Secretary" and reconcile § 5(a) with § 8 (items 6, 26) so the bill doesn't lose in court before it loses on the seabed.
